tldr: Without using any real robot data or physics simulators, the authors pretrained a Transformer entirely on synthetic data generated from purely mathematical control abstractions like MDPs and linear dynamical systems, enabling zero-shot action prediction on unseen physical robots.
overview:
The biggest bottleneck in robot learning and Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models is the extremely high cost of collecting real robot data across diverse tasks and morphologies. Physics simulators offer a cheaper data source, but building simulation environments and handling domain transfer require heavy engineering effort. To address this, the authors asked an ambitious question: "Can we learn the fundamentals of robotic control from purely mathematical data that has no physical embodiment at all?"

They focused on the action prediction task, where the model predicts the next action from a context history of states and actions. Even across vastly different robots, fundamental control principles remain shared: actions depend on states, and states change smoothly as a result of those actions. To learn this common structure, the authors generated procedural synthetic data without any embodiment based on three mathematical abstractions: Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), contextual bandits, and Linear Dynamical Systems (LDS). Feeding these into a Transformer using the Prior-Data Fitted Network (PFN) framework, the model predicts actions purely through in-context learning without any gradient updates at test time.

Evaluating on simulators (VMAS, RoboMimic) and four real-robot datasets (manipulator, wheeled vehicle, quadruped, and multicopter), the model—having never seen a robot before—achieved zero-shot prediction accuracy far exceeding random guessing. While a baseline trained on real robot data performed well on its training tasks, its performance collapsed on unseen tasks. In contrast, the proposed method showed stable generalization across entirely unseen tasks.
contributions: Demonstrated that robot behavior priors can be learned entirely from synthetic data generated from purely mathematical control abstractions (MDPs, bandits, LDS), without using any real robot or physics simulator data.
Built an in-context learning framework (PFN) that predicts actions for unseen robots immediately from a state-action context without updating model weights at inference time.

Showed that specialized control priors clearly outperform generic tabular causal priors, and identified that introducing smooth continuous dynamics (LDS) is the most critical factor for physical robot transfer.

Demonstrated that while models trained on real robot data collapse sharply on unseen tasks, a model pretrained on abstract synthetic data maintains stable zero-shot prediction capabilities across all unseen tasks.

sections.heading: Can we learn robot behavior without robot data?
sections.summary: To overcome the high cost of collecting real-world robot data, this paper proposes pretraining control priors on purely mathematical, non-embodied synthetic data. Using in-context learning, a model that has never observed a robot can perform zero-shot action prediction on unseen physical robot tasks.
sections.details:
Recent advances in Vision-Language-Action (VLA) models and generalist policies have driven major progress in robot control. However, their success relies heavily on massive physical demonstrations or simulation data. Real-world data collection remains exceptionally expensive, and even simulation requires significant engineering overhead to construct individual environments. This led the authors to ask: "Can we learn useful priors from generic data sources that completely lack robot embodiment?"

The paper focuses on action prediction, where a model infers unseen actions given a context of state-action pairs. Regardless of robot morphology, control inherently shares common structures: decisions depend on states, and states evolve smoothly over time. If a model can pretrain on these abstract dynamics, it should provide a useful foundation for unseen robots. Because this works downstream of an image encoder, it functions complementarily to representations learned from web-scale image and text data.

To test this hypothesis, the authors adopted the Prior-Data Fitted Network (PFN) framework. They procedurally generated synthetic data from three mathematical abstractions—Markov Decision Processes (MDPs), contextual bandits, and Linear Dynamical Systems (LDS)—and pretrained a Transformer. While generic tabular priors struggled to transfer to physical robots, the model equipped with specialized control priors achieved non-trivial zero-shot prediction performance on unseen real-world tasks, despite never seeing a robot during pretraining.

sections.heading: From behavioral cloning to PFNs: the research landscape
sections.summary: Prior work in behavioral cloning, simulation, and foundation models has relied on scaling real data or replicating specific physical environments. This work stands apart by extracting priors that cross embodiment boundaries using non-robotic, abstract synthetic data rather than simulating physical environments.
sections.details:
To contextualize this work, four related research areas are examined:

- Behavioral cloning (BC) and data collection: BC directly learns state-to-action mappings from expert demonstrations and is widely used across robotics. While modern approaches have grown sophisticated with diffusion policies, Transformers, and action chunking, they still depend on massive, diverse robot datasets. Data scarcity and bias remain key causes of performance degradation.
- Simulators and sim-to-real: GPU-accelerated physics simulators help mitigate the cost of physical data collection. However, these simulators aim to faithfully replicate specific target robots and environments. This work is complementary: instead of simulating particular robots, it extracts shared priors from abstract, non-robotic data.
- Robot foundation models and cross-embodiment learning: Models like $\pi_{0}$ and GR00T pool data from diverse robots to train generalist policies. Yet they still depend on large curated robot datasets or video generation. This paper starts from a different premise, asking how much prior knowledge can be acquired from cheap procedural synthetic data before the model ever observes real-world physical behavior.
- Synthetic data for in-context prediction: Prior-Data Fitted Networks (PFNs) train Transformers on synthetic data to perform inference in a single forward pass over context examples, requiring no gradient updates. While TabPFN achieved prominent success on tabular data, extensions to reinforcement learning and decision-making remained confined to simulators. This study is the first to test whether priors derived from non-embodied mathematical abstractions can transfer to physical robots.

sections.heading: Problem setting: action prediction via in-context learning
sections.summary: Robot action prediction is formulated as an in-context classification problem. Continuous action spaces are clustered into discrete tokens, and the model predicts actions for query states based on past state-action context without any gradient updates.
sections.details:
This work frames robot action prediction as a classification task solved via in-context learning.

The model $q_{\theta}$ receives a context set $D_{\text{ctx}}=\{(x_{i},y_{i})\}_{i=1}^{n}$ and query inputs $D_{\text{query}}=\{x_{j}\}_{j=1}^{m}$ simultaneously. Without updating any model parameters, it outputs the predictive distribution $q_{\theta}(y_{j}\mid x_{j},D_{\text{ctx}})$ for each query in a single forward pass. During pretraining, the model minimizes standard negative log-likelihood (NLL) over tasks (context and query pairs) sampled from a dataset prior $p_{D}$.

To handle continuous robot action spaces, the action data is tokenized into $K=64$ discrete bins using K-means clustering. The label $y$ is the index of the nearest centroid.

For evaluation, in addition to classification Accuracy and NLL, the authors introduced a new metric called Relative Centroid Distance (RCD) to evaluate how well discrete predictions preserve the continuous metric space. RCD measures the Euclidean distance between the predicted centroid $c(\hat{y}_{j})$ and the true centroid $c(y_{j})$, normalized by the expected distance under uniform random guessing. A perfect prediction yields $0.0$, while random guessing yields $1.0$, providing an intuitive check on whether the model understands spatial proximity.

sections.heading: Proposed method: generating data from mathematical control abstractions
sections.summary: The authors developed three mathematical data generators (MDPs, contextual bandits, and linear dynamical systems) that do not mimic any specific robot. A Transformer is pretrained on synthetic episodes sampled from these generators and compared against a general tabular baseline.
sections.details:
The design of the pretraining data generator $G$ is the core of this approach. The model architecture, compute budget, and training routine are kept identical across setups; only the pretraining data distribution is varied to compare transfer performance. Crucially, the order of feature dimensions is randomly shuffled for each task, preventing the model from assuming fixed semantics for any input dimension and forcing it to infer structure purely from the provided context.

### IV-A Tabular (Generic) Priors
As a baseline, the authors used the generic tabular prior from TabPFN. This static generator produces feature-label mappings using Structural Causal Models (SCMs), Bayesian Neural Networks (BNNs), or Gaussian Processes (GPs), containing no temporal structure or embodiment.

### IV-B Synthetic Control Priors
Assuming that the essence of robotic control lies in actions being chosen conditioned on states, smooth state transitions, and consistency with latent objectives, three complementary generators were designed:

- Markov Decision Processes (MDPs): Models sequential decision-making toward long-term goals. Transition and reward functions are sampled via Gaussian processes over randomly placed states, solved using finite-horizon value iteration, and sampled into episodes via a Boltzmann policy with temperature.
- Contextual Bandits: Deliberately removes temporal progression to isolate single-step associations between states and actions. Rewards are computed via a bilinear form over state and action features, and actions are chosen using a Boltzmann distribution.
- Linear Dynamical Systems (LDS): Captures the smooth state transitions with high temporal autocorrelation characteristic of physical systems. Following $x_{t+1}=Ax_{t}+b_{a}+\varepsilon$ with a diagonal decay matrix $A$ (decay rates close to 1) and action-conditioned displacements $b_a$, diverse trajectories are generated with a linear softmax policy.

None of these generators contain any robotics domain knowledge such as kinematic chains, joint limits, or sensor specifications.

sections.heading: Experimental results: validation on simulators and real robots
sections.summary: Evaluations were conducted across simulators (VMAS, RoboMimic) and four real-robot datasets. The control priors substantially outperformed the generic tabular prior. While a real-robot baseline collapsed on unseen tasks, the proposed approach showed strong generalization and stability.
sections.details:
Evaluation sampled 512 windows of up to 2000 timesteps from each dataset, using cross-fitting where half the window serves as context and the other half as queries.

### V-A & V-B Prior Evaluation
On VMAS (a multi-agent RL environment with 9 actions), the model pretrained with the proposed Control Priors achieved 58% accuracy, outperforming the generic Tabular Prior (49%) by about 9 percentage points (random guess is ~11%).
On the 64-way classification tasks in RoboMimic and four real-robot datasets (DROID manipulation, A2D2 driving, GrandTour quadruped, and multicopter flight), the performance gap widened. The tabular prior dropped near random chance (~1.6%), whereas the control priors model achieved 16% accuracy on RoboMimic and 17% on real robot data. Substantial gains were also observed in RCD, confirming that the model captured the underlying continuous action space structure.

### V-C Ablations
Training on each generator individually revealed that the Linear Dynamical System (LDS) alone was the strongest component, matching the full three-prior mixture on real robot data. In contrast, MDP and bandit priors alone lagged behind. This highlights that what matters most for physical transfer is not long-term value estimation (MDPs) or simple state-action mappings (bandits), but local continuous temporal smoothness (LDS).

### V-D Comparison with Real-Data-Trained Models
A compute-matched baseline was trained directly on a subset of real robot data. While this baseline reached 83% accuracy on in-domain tasks, its accuracy collapsed to 27% on out-of-domain tasks, dropping near random guessing. In contrast, the synthetic-prior model, treating all physical tasks as zero-shot, maintained steady, consistent prediction accuracy and outperformed the baseline on unseen tasks.

### V-E Context Length Scaling
Increasing context length from 100 to 1000 samples led to monotonic accuracy gains. This confirms that the model infers structure from context rather than relying on memorized rules. On real robot data, the scaling curve did not saturate at 1000 samples, indicating potential for further gains with longer contexts.

sections.heading: Conclusions and insights: open-loop execution and open questions
sections.summary: Non-robotic mathematical abstractions can indeed instill useful priors for robot control. Open-loop trajectory prediction produced reasonable flight paths, though notable questions remain, such as an unintuitive interaction during finetuning with real data.
sections.details:
This study provides positive empirical evidence that useful zero-shot transfer can be achieved using purely mathematical abstractions, addressing the question of whether models can learn robot behavior without robot data.

### VI-A Open-Loop State Prediction
To examine the quality of predicted actions, the authors ran an open-loop experiment integrating multicopter flight predictions over 300 timesteps (roughly 15 seconds) without state feedback. Despite the lack of corrective observations where errors compound easily, the mean position error stayed under 0.48m and peak error remained around 1m, successfully tracking the true trajectory at a practically meaningful level.

### VI-B Scale Limitations
One reason the real-data baseline collapsed on unseen tasks is the small model scale used (TabPFN architecture, ~7ms/query inference time) due to compute constraints. Because larger models like $\pi_0$ and GR00T exhibit strong cross-embodiment transfer, scaling synthetic control priors to larger architectures is an essential next step.

### VI-C Counterintuitive Finetuning Behavior
The authors anticipated that finetuning the pretrained model on small amounts of real data would outperform training from scratch. Surprisingly, while the pretrained model held an advantage with very few samples, scratch training quickly surpassed it once 1,000 to 5,000 real samples were provided. This discrepancy likely stems from the gap between pretraining (broad generalization across single-pass synthetic tasks) and optimization on real datasets (repeatedly overfitting to a fixed dataset), pointing to the need for new pipelines that reconcile both objectives.

captions.F7: Comparison of true trajectory (black line) and open-loop predicted trajectory (green line) obtained by integrating model-predicted actions over 300 steps (~15 seconds) on real multicopter flight data. Even without feedback correction from re-observing states, the model tracks the true flight path with an average error below 0.48m.

takeaways: Robot action priors can be acquired purely from mathematical control abstractions like MDPs and LDS, completely bypassing the need for physical robot data or physics simulators.
Smooth, temporally autocorrelated continuous dynamics (LDS) contributed the most to zero-shot transfer on physical robots.
In-context learning enables immediate adaptation to unseen robots and tasks without needing test-time gradient updates or finetuning.

Finetuning abstractly pretrained models on real robot data can be quickly overtaken by training from scratch, revealing an open research gap in connecting synthetic pretraining with real-world adaptation.
limitations: Absolute action prediction accuracy on real-world tasks remains modest at around 17% (out of 64 classes) for practical control applications.
Evaluations relied on a relatively small Transformer architecture due to compute constraints; whether these advantages hold at the scale of modern foundation models remains unverified.
Directly finetuning the synthetically pretrained model on small amounts of real-world data does not yield the expected performance gains, presenting an unresolved optimization challenge.
